tagline: Historic farms and village districts follow an early stagecoach line.
intro: Historic farms line the Accommodation Line Scenic Byway, with historic districts at its ends. The Federal Highway Administration’s byway account emphasizes that rural and village setting, together with recreation at lakes, rivers and two state parks. The Little Miami River flows through Waynesville and Spring Valley Township.

The road follows the Accommodation stagecoach line of the early nineteenth century. Waynesville had been laid out in 1796 and was built up chiefly by Quakers. Another form of transport shaped Spring Valley: construction of the Little Miami Railroad brought the village into being in the early 1840s, and it was platted in 1844.

Begin in Waynesville’s Main Street district, which extends from below South Street north to Franklin Road. The engine house on Chapman Street adds the story of the village’s first fire station. Continue northeast toward Spring Valley, the village that grew with the railroad.

moments.title: Waynesville Main Street
moments.text: Waynesville’s Main Street district extends for about five blocks, from just below South Street to Franklin Road. The district’s listed buildings include the 1844 Waynesville Academy and the 1847 Mahlon Bateman House, a Greek Revival building. Their dates follow the village’s beginnings: Waynesville was laid out in 1796 and built up chiefly by Quakers. When the 36-acre district entered the National Register in 2002, it included 98 buildings counted as contributing to its historic character. The Thomas Swift House adds another architectural form: a five-bay brick I-house in the Federal style.

moments.title: Waynesville Engine House and Lockup
moments.text: Fire protection and a jail shared this address on Chapman Street. The engine house was built in 1881 as Waynesville’s first fire station. In 1886 the village purchased a fire truck and added a jail extension at the back.

moments.title: Spring Valley
moments.text: Spring Valley owes its beginnings to the Little Miami Railroad. Construction through the area in the early 1840s started the settlement, which was platted in 1844. The village lies in central Spring Valley Township, through which the Little Miami River flows. Where the river crosses into Warren County, it reaches Greene County’s lowest point, 730 feet above sea level.
